title: Controlled source pack for Class 3 Water Distribution remediation
authoringRules: Use only the source keys in this pack for source metadata.
Do not invent a statute, regulation section, numeric threshold, test interval, chemical dose, contact time, certification requirement, or manufacturer practice.
If no source directly supports a specific numeric or regulatory claim, rewrite the item to test a supported qualitative principle instead.
Use Ontario sources for Ontario regulatory or operational claims. Do not cite a general technical source as Ontario law.
Each item must have one best answer, four parallel and plausible options, a concise explanation, a source title, source reference, source URL, and a blueprint objective.
Avoid absolute claims such as always, never, only, or must unless the cited source makes that claim.
Do not include a source citation in learner-facing question text or answer options. Source metadata supports internal governance.
Use the WPI blueprint only to describe the topic objective. It is not factual evidence for the answer.

sources.title: Ontario Design Guidelines for Drinking-Water Systems: Instrumentation, Control and Distribution Systems
permittedClaims: High-quality distribution systems provide continuous potable supply at adequate pressure and seek to minimize water age, dead ends, and customer inconvenience during repairs.
Positive pressure should be maintained to prevent contaminant intrusion.
Water age, flow, pipe condition, and deposited materials affect distribution-system water quality.
Interconnections and pressure zones require consideration of water quality and upstream and downstream pressure impacts.
Hydraulic analysis supports water-main sizing and pressure assessment.

At maximum day demand plus fire flow, the recommended minimum ground-level pressure is 140 kPa; normal operating pressure is approximately 350 to 480 kPa and should not be below 275 kPa; maximum pressure should not exceed 700 kPa without pressure reduction.
Rapid valve operation, pump starts, pump shutdowns, and power failures can create transient pressures.
restrictions: These are design guidelines, not a substitute for a utility-specific operating procedure or an enforceable regulation.
Do not infer a specific municipal practice or maintenance interval from this source.

sources.title: Ontario Design Guidelines for Drinking-Water Systems: Pumping Facilities and Treated Water Storage
permittedClaims: Treated-water and booster pumping stations should have appropriate firm capacity considering available pressure-zone storage and source conditions.
Pumping facilities should support water quality by minimizing retention time and maintaining appropriate flows and velocities.
Pumps, level instruments, controls, pressure, flow, storage level, and operating records are relevant to safe assessment of pumping and storage performance.
Treated-water storage should help minimize on-off cycling of treated-water pumps.
A standpipe with a booster station may have an equalization volume related to maintaining pressure in the system.
restrictions: Do not claim a universal wet-well volume, pump start limit, generator run interval, or NPSH margin unless it is expressly provided by another source.
Do not treat a standpipe as a surge tank.

sources.title: Ontario Watermain Disinfection Procedure
permittedClaims: For a new watermain, tablet or continuous-feed disinfection requires at least 24 hours at an initial chlorine concentration of at least 25 mg/L.
For a new watermain, slug disinfection requires at least 3 hours at an initial chlorine concentration of at least 100 mg/L.
For a new watermain, spray disinfection requires at least 30 minutes at an initial chlorine concentration of at least 200 mg/L.

An isolated section that did not maintain the specified disinfectant residual requires a re-commissioning plan that at minimum includes flushing and satisfactory microbiological results before return to service.
Watermain breaks are Category 2 unless an Operator-in-Charge visually inspects and classifies the break as Category 1 based on the procedure.
restrictions: Distinguish new-watermain procedures from emergency repair procedures.
Do not substitute an AWWA method, concentration, or contact time for the Ontario procedure.

sources.title: O. Reg. 632/05: Confined Spaces
permittedClaims: Acceptable oxygen content is at least 19.5 percent and not more than 23 percent by volume.
A separate entry permit is required before work is performed in a confined space.
An entry permit includes identified hazards, controls, equipment, rescue information, and atmospheric test results.
Adequate atmospheric tests must be performed as often as necessary before and while workers are in the confined space to ensure acceptable atmospheric levels are maintained.
Testing must use calibrated instruments appropriate for the identified hazards.
restrictions: Do not state that continuous monitoring is required in every confined-space situation.

sources.title: O. Reg. 213/91: Construction Projects
permittedClaims: Water mains are included in the regulation's definition of conduit.
Excavation work is governed by Part III of the Construction Projects regulation, including requirements concerning entry, soil types, precautions, general requirements, and support systems.

A competent worker is qualified by knowledge, training, and experience, is familiar with applicable occupational health and safety requirements, and knows the potential or actual dangers related to the work.
restrictions: Do not invent trench-depth, slope, shoring, or protective-system thresholds without a direct verified citation.

sources.title: O. Reg. 169/03: Ontario Drinking Water Quality Standards
permittedClaims: E. coli is not detectable under the microbiological standard.
Total coliforms are not detectable under the microbiological standard.
Where water does not meet a standard, the regulation describes immediate contact with the medical officer of health and directed steps, and links corrective action to O. Reg. 170/03 schedules.
restrictions: Do not use this source to claim that a cross-connection program is mandated by O. Reg. 170/03.
Do not state an adverse-result notification workflow beyond the text in this source.

sources.title: O. Reg. 128/04: Certification of Drinking Water System Operators and Water Quality Analysts
permittedClaims: A municipal residential subsystem must have an overall responsible operator holding a certificate for the subsystem type and class equal to or higher than the subsystem class.
Class III certificate qualifications include passing an approved examination, holding the relevant Class II certificate, and specified education and experience requirements.
restrictions: Do not create questions about an exact applicant profile unless the full regulatory text directly supports every condition used.

sources.title: EPA EPANET: Application for Modeling Drinking Water Distribution Systems
permittedClaims: EPANET models pressurized pipe networks with pipes, junctions, pumps, valves, tanks, and reservoirs.
It can model pressure, flow, tank level, water age, water quality, pumps, valves, friction head loss, minor losses, and pressure-dependent demands.
Hydraulic modeling can support planning, pump and tank operations, water quality assessment, fire-flow analysis, emergency preparation, and model calibration.
restrictions: Use basic hydraulic equations only where they are shown in the item and can be independently checked.
Do not cite EPANET as an Ontario regulatory source.

sources.title: EPA Distribution System Water Quality: Protecting Water Quality Through Water Age Management
permittedClaims: Water age is the time water spends in the distribution system before use.
Excessive water age can contribute to disinfectant residual consumption, DBP formation, microbial growth, sediment, and water-quality deterioration.
Dead ends, closed valves, poor circulation, oversized assets, and thermal stratification can increase water age.
Useful operational responses include residual monitoring, water-quality or hydraulic modeling, controlled flushing, optimizing tank and pumping operations, and checking valve positions.
restrictions: Do not use this U.S. guidance to assert Ontario legal requirements.

sources.title: AWWA Water Loss Control
permittedClaims: Real losses arise from pipeline leakage.
Apparent losses occur when customer consumption is not properly measured or billed.
The IWA/AWWA water-audit method is a best-practice tool used to manage water loss and revenue recovery.
A water audit is a rational starting point for water-loss control and leakage-management decisions.
restrictions: Do not use non-revenue water and unaccounted-for water as interchangeable terms unless the item defines its terminology.

sources.title: Water Professionals International Class III Water Distribution Need-to-Know Criteria
permittedClaims: Use only to map the question to a Class III distribution subject area such as components, operation and maintenance, water quality, safety, administration, or public interactions.
restrictions: This source does not establish the factual correctness of an answer.
